Alderney is the most northerly located of the Channel Islands. It is part of Bailiwick of Guernsey, British Crown dependency. Alderney Island is 5 km (3 miles) long and 2.4 km (1 1⁄2 miles) wide. Its area is 8 km2 (3 sq.miles), making it the 3rd-largest of the Channel Islands, and the 2nd largest in Bailiwick.

Alderney is around 15 km (10 miles) to the west of La Hague on Cotentin Peninsula, Normandy (France), 30 km (20 miles) to the north-east of Guernsey, 100 km (60 miles) from the south coast of Great Britain. Alderney is the closest of Channel Islands to both the United Kingdom and France. It is separated by the dangerous Alderney Race from Cap de la Hague.

Alderney Island cruise terminal

Cruise ships to Alderney Island Channel Islands dock (anchor) at St Anne - port town on the northern coast.

Alderney is small enough for a rewarding independent port day, but the arrival is by tender and much of the island is hilly. Braye Harbour, St Anne and nearby coastal sights are practical on foot; reaching the eastern beaches, lighthouse and more distant fortifications is easier by pre-booked taxi, bicycle or tour.

At a Glance

  • Overall: Independent with some planning or transport.
  • Arrival: Cruise ships normally anchor off Braye Harbour and tender passengers to the harbour's passenger landing pontoon. There is no dedicated cruise terminal.
  • St Anne: About 1.1 km (0.7 mi) from the harbour, typically a 15–20 minute walk uphill.
  • Best for: Coastal walking, Victorian and WWII fortifications, beaches, wildlife and the compact center of St Anne.
  • Main limitation: Taxis are limited and should be arranged in advance when possible. Tender operations can also be affected by wind and sea conditions.

Getting from the Cruise Port

Ship tenders use the passenger landing pontoon at Braye Harbour, close to the Harbour Master's Office. Passengers step directly into the working harbour area, with Braye Beach and the lower end of Braye Road nearby.

St Anne is uphill from the harbour. The walk is short enough for most passengers, but the climb is noticeable and some streets in town are cobbled. Allow approximately 15–20 minutes each way between the harbour and central Victoria Street.

Alderney does not have the frequent public transport normally found at larger cruise ports. Licensed taxis are available but supply is limited, so relying on finding one immediately at the harbour is not advisable. Bicycle and e-bike hire can be useful for passengers wanting to cover more of the island.

The Alderney Railway runs between Braye and Mannez on selected days, normally including Saturdays during the main summer season. Its limited timetable makes it an attraction rather than dependable cruise-day transport, so check the operating schedule for the date of the call.

Best Ways to Spend Your Time

St Anne and the Historic Town Center

Allow: 2–3 hours. Independent: Easy, provided you are comfortable with the uphill approach.

Walk from Braye Harbour into St Anne and explore Victoria Street, St Anne's Church, the older lanes around Le Bourgage and the central streets. The Alderney Museum is a worthwhile addition for passengers interested in the island's evacuation, occupation, fortifications and local history.

This is the most straightforward choice for a short call because no transport is necessary and the route can easily be shortened if tender operations or weather change.

Braye Harbour and Beach

Allow: 1–2 hours. Independent: Very easy.

Passengers wanting a relaxed visit can remain close to the tender landing. Braye Beach is only a few minutes away and is sheltered by the harbour breakwater. Combine the beach with a walk around the harbour, Braye Common and views toward the surrounding coastal defenses.

This is also the safest option when the call is short or tendering conditions appear uncertain because you remain close to the return point.

Fort Albert, Bibette Head and the North Coast

Allow: About 2.5–3 hours with sightseeing stops. Independent: Practical for reasonably fit walkers.

The official Fort Albert and Bibette Head walking route covers approximately 5.3 km (3.3 mi). It passes Braye Common, viewpoints above Braye Bay, the Fort Albert area and well-preserved German defenses at Bibette Head before continuing through the northern coastal landscape.

The route includes hills, tracks and exposed sections. Walking shoes and a windproof or waterproof layer are advisable even when conditions at the harbour appear calm.

Longis Bay, Roman Fort and Mannez

Allow: 3–4 hours. Independent: Best with a bicycle or pre-arranged taxi.

The eastern side of Alderney combines Longis Bay, nature areas, the Roman Fort and the coast around Mannez. Longis has the island's longest sandy beach and is also useful when northerly winds make the north-coast beaches less comfortable.

Trying to include all of these sights entirely on foot can consume too much of a normal port call. Cycling works well on Alderney's relatively quiet roads, while a taxi or local tour gives more time at each stop.

Wildlife or Island Boat Trip

Allow: Usually around 2.5–3 hours depending on the operator and conditions. Organized excursion recommended.

Local boat trips can explore Alderney's cliffs, forts and offshore seabird areas, including the gannet colony around Les Etacs and, seasonally, wildlife around Burhou. These trips are strongly dependent on weather and sea conditions and should be reserved in advance rather than treated as an activity that can always be arranged after landing.

Self-Guided Walking Tours

Braye Harbour and Beach Walk — Easy

Distance: Approximately 2 km (1.2 mi) return. Pure walking time: About 30–40 minutes. Recommended time: 1–1.5 hours. Difficulty: Easy and mostly level.

  1. Start at the passenger landing pontoon beside the Harbour Master's Office.
  2. Walk through the harbour area and look across Braye Harbour toward the Victorian breakwater.
  3. Continue to Braye Beach.
  4. Follow the shore toward Braye Common.
  5. Pass Braye Station, the western terminus of the Alderney Railway.
  6. Return along the harbour side to the tender pontoon.

This route keeps you close to the ship and is useful for passengers with a short visit or when changing weather makes a longer walk undesirable.

Braye Harbour and St Anne — Moderate

Distance: Approximately 4 km (2.5 mi) including a circuit of central St Anne. Pure walking time: About 60–75 minutes. Recommended time: 2–3 hours. Difficulty: Moderate because of the sustained climb from Braye and some cobbled streets.

  1. Start at the Braye Harbour passenger landing pontoon.
  2. Walk inland and follow Braye Road uphill toward St Anne.
  3. Reach Victoria Street and the Visitor Information Centre area.
  4. Visit St Anne's Church.
  5. Continue through the old streets around Connaught Square and Le Bourgage.
  6. Pass the Alderney Museum if time permits.
  7. Return to Victoria Street and walk downhill along Braye Road.
  8. Finish back at the passenger landing pontoon.

The town portion follows the same compact area covered by Alderney's official self-guided St Anne walk. Allow additional time if visiting the church or museum.

Beaches and Nature

Braye Beach is the easiest beach for cruise passengers because it is immediately beside the harbour and requires no transport.

Longis Bay offers a much longer sandy shoreline on the southeast coast and combines well with the Roman Fort and nearby nature reserve. A bicycle, taxi or tour is preferable for a time-limited port call.

Saye, Arch and Corblets are attractive north-coast beaches but are farther from the tender landing. They are more practical as part of a cycling trip, taxi circuit or longer coastal walk.

Platte Saline should not be treated as a swimming beach because of its severe undercurrent.

When a Tour Makes More Sense

A guided taxi or minibus circuit is worthwhile for passengers who want to see several parts of the island without spending much of the call walking between them. A typical island circuit can combine St Anne, Longis, the Roman Fort, Mannez, north-coast fortifications and scenic viewpoints.

Organized or pre-booked arrangements are particularly sensible for boat trips and for passengers with limited mobility. Alderney's small taxi fleet means spontaneous transport cannot be assumed to be available when a cruise ship is visiting.

Practical Tips

  • Confirm the ship's exact last tender time before leaving the vessel. It may be substantially earlier than the published departure time.
  • For independent sightseeing around St Anne, aim to be back near Braye Harbour at least 30–45 minutes before the last tender; allow a larger margin after longer island trips.
  • Do not plan an itinerary that depends on finding an unreserved taxi for the return journey.
  • Coastal weather can change quickly. Carry a light waterproof or windproof layer on longer walks.
  • Check tides before exploring rock pools, causeways or low-lying coastal areas.
  • Some shops and services close at lunchtime, and Wednesday afternoon opening can be limited.
  • If the ship announces deteriorating tender conditions or an earlier final tender, return to Braye Harbour promptly.
